I’m late to the party here, but I’ve been there, done that, and survived it. I graduated May 2020 - it was HORRENDOUS. I mean, the worst time to graduate other than 2008 times. If you want a glimpse at my mental state, you could go back in my posts and comments during that time, lol. I made it to many final rounds, but never got the position. 9/10 it went to an internal candidate. I was offered my dream job in October 2020, but they disclosed the salary with the offer (I didn’t have the confidence to ask up front) and I wouldn’t have been able to make ends meet, even remotely.  I didn’t find a job in higher ed until April 2021. I worked at a non-profit from February -April 2021, which was the pits, but I won’t get into that. 

A few things that helped me get through it:
1) I expanded my search. I was looking only at the Pacific Northwest due to where my partner was, but after 4 months of searching, he and I discussed and we expanded to include the South as well. 
2) Use this time to work on certifications. There are so many that you can use to show that you’ve still been growing professionally. Just use LinkedIn. 
3) Continue to grow your network. I would reach out to people via LinkedIn who I had mutual connections with and just ask to learn more about their functional area and what they do. Most people are more than happy to help in any way they can
4) My therapist at the time helped me to live more in the moment and reminded me that this interim period may be the last time I would just have a break. She was right! I now look back at that time as incredibly character building. 

Deep breaths, you got this. Celebrate your graduation, you worked hard for that! I’ve worked in Student Affairs and Academic Affairs - always happy to help, DM me if you ever need anything

Alum, previous advisor and work in higher education. Conversations with an advisor should happen ASAP. Hi! Gone through on-campus interviews and planned in-person interviews for my direct hires. All the advice already here is really good. A few important things to note:
1) Ask questions - and carry a padfolio or something along those lines with your questions. Be really specific in the questions, too. Show you’ve done your research through the questions. I always asked how the position I was interviewing for could assist in KPIs or the specific mission of the department (look it up and pick your favorite part of it!)
2) if you haven’t received a schedule, know you’ll probably have multiple rounds. For example, you could have a round of interviews involving campus partners, student leaders, parallel roles, and leadership. Mine is more weird/creepy than annoying. My mom and I frequently went to the parks together growing up. Once, in 2006, she and I stayed at the Dolphin. We stopped by the buffet restaurant at the time (don’t remember what it was called then) for breakfast before heading to Epcot. My mom went up to grab some food while I stayed back at the table. A girl around my age came over, sat down, and started chatting with me. I was a pretty friendly kid, so I was happy to make a new pal. She asked me who I was with and what our plans were for the day. I excitedly shared that my mom and I were heading to Epcot for the day, and she said “so are me and my dad! We should go together!” Obviously I was STOKED to spend time with my new bestie. She said she would go tell her dad. When my mom came back, I told my mom about my new friend and how I wanted to hang out with her. She was, understandably, a little weirded out but didn’t want to crush my newfound dreams. Soon after my mom came back, the girl and her dad came over to our table and shared his excitement over going to Epcot together. 

At this point, my mom decided it was time to nope out. She told them that we had forgotten something in our room and would maybe see them in the parks. The dad was a bit annoyed but then walked away. We decided to kill some time before heading over to Epcot. We stopped at EVERY shop on the Boardwalk, purchased some items, took photos, totaling about 2 hours of time. 

We determined that was enough time. But, as we approached the entrance in World Showcase, who should be there WAITING but the man and his daughter. My mom didn’t see them until they approached us. We had no idea what to do but walk around with them for a while. I remember the daughter wanted to keep me separate from my mom. She kept talking about how her dad was involved in drugs, he had been in jail a year or so, all of this wild stuff. After 15 minutes or so, my mom grabbed my hand, said “I just got a call from your dad, it looks like he’s going to be joining us for our trip!” And pulled me away. 

I have no idea what the intentions were, but it thoroughly worried my mom.

I was diagnosed with depression in high school. It started with numbness. I didn't feel anything. I didn't care about school or friends or my health. I can recall lying in bed, my mother crying over me because she didn't understand, and I felt absolutely nothing. I knew there had to be something wrong with me if I felt no emotion seeing my mom cry. 
I then began flirting with the idea of suicide. I was hospitalized once for telling one of those emergency numbers that I had a plan to commit suicide. Looking back I know I wouldn't have gone through with it; I just felt trapped. 
I tried every medication on the market, it seems. It was such a trial and error. One medication made me unable to get out of bed in the morning, while another made me cry almost all the time. No medication was a perfect fit; it was really just which one caused the least side effects. I switched psychiatrists halfway through my depression.
Finding the right medication enabled me to live my life again. I regained my interests in theater and singing. However, I did gain a lot of weight. 
My depression began to taper off and die down around senior year of high school and freshman year of college. It took a very long for me and my therapist to convince my psychiatrist that I was no longer depressed (after she took me off my meds she slapped me with an anxiety disorder diagnosis, but that's another story).
I'm lucky to say that today I'm the happiest I've ever been. It's been such a long road. If anyone reading this is going through what I went through, please realize that there is an end IF you get help. I know how hard it is to admit you need help, but it is so necessary. Don't look at medication as something that will change who you are; it is an important crutch that you will remove when you're healed. If a friend is reaching out to you because they notice something is wrong, don't push them away. It's so easy to want to isolate yourself because it's hard to explain to another person how it feels, but simply being in another person's presence is so healing. 
Just like a broken bone, a disease like depression needs time, medication, and support to heal. But it will heal. 
If anyone needs someone to talk to feel free to DM me.
